title: Chemistry of living beings & water
outcomes: Properties of water and hydrogen bonds
Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect

summary.overview: Life is chemistry in water. Carbon builds the molecular skeletons; the 3D shape of those molecules (stereochemistry) decides how they interact; and water, through hydrogen bonds and the hydrophobic effect, shapes every protein, membrane and nucleic acid.

sections.heading: Carbon and oxidation state
points: Of about 30 essential elements, C, H, O, N, P and S dominate; metal ions (K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺) have key roles in metabolism.
Carbon forms four stable covalent bonds (single, double or triple) with C, H, O and N, giving chains, rings and branched 3D structures.
Oxidation state of carbon: CH4 (most reduced) → alcohol → aldehyde/ketone → carboxylic acid → CO2 (most oxidised).
The more reduced the carbon, the more energy it releases when fully oxidised, which is why fats yield more energy per gram than sugars.

sections.heading: Isomerism and stereochemistry
points: Stereoisomers have the same bonds but a different 3D arrangement.
Geometric (cis/trans) isomers differ in physical and chemical properties, e.g. fumarate (trans) vs maleate (cis).
A chiral carbon carries four different substituents; n chiral centres give up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers.
Enantiomers are mirror images: they have identical physical properties except the direction they rotate plane-polarised light, and they react identically with achiral reagents.
Diastereomers are non-mirror-image stereoisomers with different physical and chemical properties.
Binding sites in biomolecules are chiral, so binding is stereospecific: two enantiomers of a drug can act very differently.

sections.heading: Water and hydrogen bonds
points: Organisms are 70–90% water; most biochemical reactions occur in water.
O is sp³ hybridised (distorted tetrahedron) and more electronegative than H, so water is a dipole that can donate and accept H-bonds.
Each water molecule can form up to four H-bonds, explaining water's high boiling point, melting point and surface tension.
H-bonds (≈ 20 kJ/mol) are much weaker than covalent O–H bonds (≈ 420 kJ/mol) and strongest when the three atoms are in a line.
Ice has the maximum number of H-bonds in an open hexagonal lattice, so it is less dense than liquid water and floats.
Water dissolves charged and polar solutes (salts, amino acids, sugars) but not non-polar ones (lipid chains, aromatic rings, gases).

sections.heading: Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect
points: Ionic (Coulombic) interactions occur between charges; dipole interactions between polar groups.

Van der Waals interactions occur between all atoms: London dispersion attraction at 0.4–0.7 nm and steric repulsion at very short distance. They are weak individually but give steric complementarity and DNA base stacking.
The hydrophobic effect is not an attraction between non-polar groups: water forms ordered, low-entropy shells around them.
When non-polar groups cluster (protein cores, micelles, membranes, steroid binding), ordered water is released and entropy increases.

keyTerms.definition: Carbon atom bonded to four different groups.
Stereoisomers that are not mirror images, including cis/trans isomers.
Attraction between an H on an electronegative atom and a lone pair on another electronegative atom.
Weak attraction (dispersion) and repulsion (steric) between any two nearby atoms.
Clustering of non-polar groups in water, driven by the increase in entropy of the released water.
Having both polar and non-polar regions, e.g. membrane lipids.

examTips: The hydrophobic effect is driven by the ENTROPY of water, not by an attraction between non-polar molecules.
Enantiomers differ only in optical rotation and in interactions with OTHER chiral molecules, such as enzymes and receptors.
Cis/trans isomers are diastereomers, not enantiomers.
More reduced carbon (more C–H bonds) means more energy released on oxidation.

questions.stem: Why is carbon able to form the backbone of so many different biomolecules?

options.text: It forms four stable covalent bonds (single, double or triple) with C, H, O and N, giving chains and rings
options.why: Its four strong bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement allow huge structural diversity.

options.text: It forms mainly ionic bonds, which break and re-form easily, so atoms can be rearranged into new molecules
options.why: Carbon forms covalent bonds, not ionic ones.

options.text: It is the most electronegative element in biology, so it pulls electrons from the atoms it bonds to
options.why: Oxygen and nitrogen are more electronegative than carbon.

options.text: It is the most abundant atom in water and body fluids, so it is readily available to cells for building
options.why: Water contains no carbon.

questions.stem: In which molecule is the carbon atom most oxidised?

options.text: Carbon dioxide (CO2)
options.why: In CO2 carbon has given up the most electron density to oxygen; it is the fully oxidised end product of metabolism.

options.text: Methane (CH4)
options.why: Methane carbon is the most reduced: it is bonded only to hydrogen.

options.text: Ethanol (CH3–CH2–OH)
options.why: An alcohol carbon is only slightly oxidised.

options.text: Acetaldehyde (CH3–CHO)
options.why: An aldehyde carbon is intermediate; it can still be oxidised to a carboxylic acid and then to CO2.

questions.stem: Why does a gram of body fat store about twice as much energy as a gram of glycogen?

options.text: Fatty-acid carbons are more reduced (mostly –CH2–), so their oxidation passes more electrons to O2
options.why: Sugar carbons already carry –OH groups (partly oxidised); fat chains have far more C–H bonds to oxidise.

options.text: Fats contain more oxygen atoms per carbon than sugars, so more oxygen is available to burn each carbon
options.why: The reverse is true: sugars are oxygen-rich, fats are oxygen-poor.

options.text: Fat is stored together with more water than glycogen, and that water adds to the energy released
options.why: The reverse: glycogen is stored with lots of water, fat with almost none. That makes fat an even better store, but it isn't why fat's fuel yields more energy.

options.text: Fatty acids contain high-energy phosphate bonds that release extra free energy when they are hydrolysed
options.why: Fatty acids contain no phosphoanhydride bonds.

questions.stem: Which property differs between the two enantiomers of a chiral compound?

options.text: The direction in which they rotate plane-polarised light
options.why: Enantiomers have identical physical properties except their interaction with polarised light (and with other chiral molecules).

options.text: Their melting point and boiling point when pure
options.why: Enantiomers have identical melting points.

options.text: Their solubility in water and in organic solvents
options.why: Water is achiral, so both enantiomers dissolve equally.

options.text: Their rate of reaction with an achiral reagent such as water
options.why: Enantiomers react identically with achiral reagents.

questions.stem: Fumarate (trans) is an intermediate of the citric acid cycle, whereas maleate (cis) is not used by the cycle. How are these two molecules related?

options.text: Geometric (cis/trans) isomers: diastereomers with different physical and chemical properties
options.why: Rotation about the C=C double bond is blocked, so cis and trans forms are distinct compounds, and enzymes distinguish them.

options.text: Enantiomers: non-superimposable mirror images with identical physical properties in water
options.why: Cis/trans isomers are not mirror images.

options.text: The same molecule drawn in two ways, which interconvert freely by rotation about the C=C bond
options.why: The double bond prevents interconversion, so they are different molecules.

options.text: Constitutional isomers: same formula, but the atoms are joined in a different order
options.why: They have the same bonds; only the spatial arrangement differs.

questions.stem: A molecule has two different chiral centres. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers it can have?

options.why: Each chiral centre has two configurations, so the maximum is 2ⁿ = 2² = 4.
Two stereoisomers arise from one chiral centre.
Eight would require three chiral centres.
Sixteen would require four chiral centres.

questions.stem: Why can the two enantiomers of a drug have very different effects in an animal, even though they have the same physical properties?

options.text: Receptors and enzymes are chiral, so their binding sites fit one enantiomer much better
options.why: Chiral binding pockets distinguish mirror images, like a right glove fitting a right hand.

options.text: One enantiomer is usually much more soluble in blood, so it reaches the tissues at a much higher concentration
options.why: Enantiomers have identical solubility in achiral solvents such as water.

options.text: One enantiomer carries an extra functional group that the other lacks, which changes its action
options.why: Enantiomers contain exactly the same groups.

options.text: The liver converts most drugs into its cis isomer, and only one enantiomer can be converted
options.why: Cis/trans isomerism is unrelated to the effects of enantiomers.

questions.outcome: Properties of water and hydrogen bonds
questions.stem: Why can one water molecule take part in up to four hydrogen bonds?

options.text: It has two H atoms to donate and two lone pairs on oxygen to accept
options.why: Water is both an H-bond donor and acceptor, arranged roughly tetrahedrally.

options.text: Oxygen forms four covalent bonds, two with its own H atoms and two with neighbouring water molecules
options.why: Oxygen makes only two covalent bonds; H-bonds are non-covalent.

options.text: Water molecules are non-polar and attract each other by dispersion
options.why: Water is strongly polar; its dipole drives the H-bonding.

options.text: Each hydrogen atom can accept two lone pairs from neighbouring oxygens, giving four bonds in all
options.why: Each H donates once; the lone pairs on O are the acceptors.

questions.outcome: Properties of water and hydrogen bonds
questions.stem: Why does ice float on liquid water?

options.text: In ice each molecule is H-bonded in an open hexagonal lattice, so molecules are further apart than in liquid
options.why: The ordered lattice is less dense, so ponds freeze from the top and life survives underneath.

options.text: Ice contains fewer hydrogen bonds than liquid water, so its molecules are held less tightly and spread out
options.why: Ice has the maximum number of H-bonds per molecule.

options.text: Freezing breaks the covalent O–H bonds, and the free H and O atoms take up more space than whole molecules
options.why: Covalent bonds are unchanged by freezing.

options.text: Ice traps tiny air bubbles as it forms, and this trapped air makes it lighter than the liquid
options.why: Even pure, bubble-free ice is less dense than liquid water.

questions.outcome: Properties of water and hydrogen bonds
questions.stem: Which statement about hydrogen bonds is correct?

options.text: They are strongest when the donor, the hydrogen and the acceptor lie in a straight line
options.why: Linear geometry gives the best overlap of the dipole interaction.

options.text: They are about as strong as a covalent O–H bond, which is why water has such a high boiling point
options.why: ≈ 20 kJ/mol vs ≈ 420 kJ/mol: about 20 times weaker.

options.text: They form only between carbon and hydrogen atoms, as in the C–H groups of fatty-acid tails
options.why: H-bonds involve electronegative atoms, usually N and O.

options.text: They are irreversible once formed, so the hydrogen bonds in liquid water are permanent
options.why: They constantly form and break at body temperature.

questions.outcome: Properties of water and hydrogen bonds
questions.stem: Why does NaCl dissolve readily in water but not in hexane?

options.text: Water dipoles surround (hydrate) Na⁺ and Cl⁻, weakening the ionic attraction; hexane cannot
options.why: Hydration shells compensate for breaking the ionic lattice; a non-polar solvent cannot do this.

options.text: Water forms covalent bonds with Na⁺, pulling it out of the crystal; hexane forms no bonds at all
options.why: Ion–dipole interactions are non-covalent.

options.text: Hexane is too acidic: its protons neutralise the Cl⁻ ions and so the crystal cannot break apart
options.why: Hexane is a non-polar hydrocarbon, not an acid.

options.text: NaCl is non-polar, so it dissolves in polar water only once its crystal has been heated
options.why: NaCl is ionic, the opposite of non-polar.

questions.outcome: Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect
questions.stem: Which statement about van der Waals interactions is correct?

options.text: They are weak individually, but many together give steric complementarity and DNA base stacking
options.why: Attraction dominates at 0.4–0.7 nm, repulsion at very short distance; the sum of many contacts is significant.

options.text: They occur only between oppositely charged ions, which is why they hold salt crystals together
options.why: Those are ionic (Coulombic) interactions.

options.text: They are stronger than covalent bonds, which is why they hold the atoms of a molecule together
options.why: They are among the weakest interactions in biology.

options.text: They are purely repulsive, so they only stop atoms coming too close and do not attract them
options.why: They have an attractive (dispersion) component and a repulsive (steric) component.

questions.outcome: Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect
questions.stem: What is the main driving force for amphipathic lipids to form micelles in water?

options.text: The entropy of water rises: ordered water around the tails is released when the tails cluster
options.why: The hydrophobic effect is entropic: fewer water molecules are ordered once tails are hidden.

options.text: Strong direct attraction between the non-polar tails, which pulls them together into the core
options.why: Dispersion between tails is weak; there is no special hydrophobic 'force'.

options.text: Covalent bonds that form between the lipid tails, locking them into the centre of the micelle
options.why: Micelles are held together non-covalently.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds between the non-polar tails, which hold the hydrocarbon chains side by side
options.why: Hydrocarbon tails cannot form hydrogen bonds.

questions.outcome: Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect
questions.stem: A steroid hormone binds a hydrophobic pocket in its receptor. Why is this binding thermodynamically favourable?

options.text: The steroid displaces ordered water from the pocket and from around itself, raising entropy
options.why: This is the hydrophobic effect at work in ligand binding, and drug designers exploit it.

options.text: The steroid forms many ionic bonds with charged groups lining the pocket, releasing a lot of heat
options.why: Steroids are largely non-polar and uncharged.

options.text: Water molecules become covalently attached to the steroid, anchoring it firmly inside the pocket
options.why: Water is released, not attached.

options.text: The pocket is filled with ice-like water that attracts the steroid and holds it in place
options.why: Ordered water is unfavourable and is pushed out by the ligand.

questions.outcome: Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect
questions.stem: Inside a folded protein, a positively charged Lys side chain sits next to a negatively charged Glu side chain. Which interaction holds them together?

options.text: An ionic (Coulombic) interaction, also called a salt bridge
options.why: Electrostatic attraction between permanent opposite charges.

options.text: A van der Waals interaction only, since the charges cancel out
options.why: Van der Waals contacts exist, but the dominant interaction is between the charges.

options.text: A covalent peptide bond between the two side chains
options.why: Side chains are not joined by peptide bonds.

options.text: The hydrophobic effect, as both side chains avoid water
options.why: Charged side chains are hydrophilic.

flashcards.front: Six most common elements in biomolecules?
flashcards.back: C, H, O, N, P, S, plus essential metal ions (K⁺, Na⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Zn²⁺, Fe²⁺).

flashcards.front: Order of carbon oxidation, least to most?
flashcards.back: Alkane (CH4) → alcohol → aldehyde/ketone → carboxylic acid → CO2.
Enantiomers: mirror images, identical physical properties except optical rotation. Diastereomers: not mirror images, different properties (includes cis/trans).

flashcards.front: Chiral centre? Maximum stereoisomers for n centres?
flashcards.back: A carbon with four different substituents. Up to 2ⁿ stereoisomers.

flashcards.outcome: Properties of water and hydrogen bonds
flashcards.back: Electronegative O, bent (distorted tetrahedral, sp³) shape, so it is a net dipole: both H-bond donor and acceptor.

flashcards.outcome: Properties of water and hydrogen bonds
flashcards.front: H-bond vs covalent O–H bond energy?
flashcards.back: ≈ 20 kJ/mol vs ≈ 420 kJ/mol. H-bonds are strongest when linear.

flashcards.outcome: Properties of water and hydrogen bonds
flashcards.back: Maximal H-bonding in an open hexagonal lattice, so it is less dense than liquid water.

flashcards.outcome: Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect
flashcards.back: Ionic (Coulombic), dipole (incl. H-bonds), van der Waals, and the hydrophobic effect.

flashcards.outcome: Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect
flashcards.back: The entropy gain of water released from ordered shells when non-polar groups cluster. It is not a direct attraction.

flashcards.outcome: Non-covalent interactions and the hydrophobic effect
flashcards.front: Where does the hydrophobic effect matter?
flashcards.back: Protein folding, protein–protein association, micelles and membranes, binding of steroid hormones and many drugs.
